```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(reiod)
grp <- eiod_age_sex_group(eiod_demo$age, eiod_demo$sex)
```

**The question:** is this diet below the per capita daily share of a planetary
boundary?

The cut-offs are Table 3 of the methods paper — one absolute threshold per
indicator per demographic group, 56 numbers in all. The result is `1` if the
diet is below its threshold, `0` if at or above it.

This article assumes you have run `vignette("data-checks")` and have a `grp`
vector from `vignette("demographic-groups")`:

```{r}
grp <- eiod_age_sex_group(eiod_demo$age, eiod_demo$sex)
```

## A. One value

Useful for checking the package against the printed table by hand. Pass
length-one vectors:

```{r}
# a 40-year-old man, 2.1 kg CO2eq for the day — group 4
eiod_absolute_threshold(2.1, group = 4, indicator = "ghg")
```

```{r}
# the number it was compared against
eiod_lookup_cutoff("ghg", group = 4, metric = "abs")
```

So `2.1 < 1.0836...` is false, and the result is `0`. The comparison is
**strict** — the published cut-offs carry a `<` sign, so a diet sitting
exactly on the threshold is coded `0`, not `1`.

## B. One vector (a column from your data)

The ordinary case. `reiod` has no dependencies, so the API is plain vectors:
you pass `df$column`, not `column`.

```{r}
ghg_ok <- eiod_absolute_threshold(eiod_demo$ghg_kgco2e, grp, "ghg")
table(ghg_ok, useNA = "ifany")
```

```{r}
round(100 * mean(ghg_ok, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
```

Read as: *"22.2% of one-day diets fall below the absolute per capita daily
threshold established for greenhouse gas emissions."*

### The indicator key and your column name are different things

Note what that call does **not** say. `"ghg"` is the indicator key `reiod`
knows; `ghg_kgco2e` is what the column happens to be called in this dataset.
They are separate things and have never had to match.

This is worth stating because it is easy to conclude otherwise. The demo data
used to have columns named `ghg`, `biodiv`, `landtotal` — the keys themselves
— which made a tidy-looking loop possible and taught people that a rename was
required. It never was. The columns were renamed in October 2026 for exactly
that reason.

## C. Adding the result as a new column

```{r}
d <- eiod_demo
d$group   <- eiod_age_sex_group(d$age, d$sex)
d$abs_ghg <- eiod_absolute_threshold(d$ghg_kgco2e, d$group, "ghg")

head(d[, c("id", "age", "sex", "group", "ghg_kgco2e", "abs_ghg")], 5)
```

Two or three columns at a time, the same way:

```{r}
d$abs_water  <- eiod_absolute_threshold(d$water_litres, d$group, "water")
d$abs_biodiv <- eiod_absolute_threshold(d$biodiv_pdf,   d$group, "biodiv")

round(100 * colMeans(d[, c("abs_ghg", "abs_water", "abs_biodiv")],
                     na.rm = TRUE), 1)
```

## D. Several indicators in one call

State the mapping once — the **name** is the indicator key, the **value** is
your column — and pass it to `eiod_absolute_all()`:

```{r}
eiod_demo_map
```

```{r}
abs_all <- eiod_absolute_all(eiod_demo, grp, eiod_demo_map)
round(100 * colMeans(abs_all, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
```

For your own data the line is the same shape:

```r
my_map <- c(ghg = "ghg_total_kg", biodiv = "pdf_year", water = "water_l")
```

## E. Only the indicators you have

**Supply any subset.** Indicators you do not name are simply absent from the
result; there is no need to have all seven, and nothing is computed for the
ones you leave out.

```{r}
two <- c(landtotal = "land_total_m2yr", water = "water_litres")
res <- eiod_absolute_all(eiod_demo, grp, map = two)

str(res)
round(100 * colMeans(res, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
```

One indicator alone works too:

```{r}
head(eiod_absolute_all(eiod_demo, grp, map = c(water = "water_litres")), 3)
```

The batch form is a loop and nothing more — it gives exactly what the
single-indicator calls give:

```{r}
identical(res$abs_water,
          eiod_absolute_threshold(eiod_demo$water_litres, grp, "water"))
```

Binding a subset straight onto your data frame:

```{r}
d2 <- cbind(eiod_demo, eiod_absolute_all(eiod_demo, grp, map = two))
names(d2)
```

Rename the output prefix with `prefix =` if `abs_` collides with something you
already have.

## Which number was each respondent compared against?

Per group:

```{r}
eiod_lookup_cutoff("ghg", metric = "abs")
```

Those are printed to 15 significant digits on purpose. The published cut-offs
need up to 14, and R's default `options(digits = 7)` would show
`1726.3821057877` as `1726.382`, which looks as though the package had rounded
the guideline. It had not — only the display was short. The `as printed`
column is the literal text transcribed from the paper, so you can check it
character for character rather than trusting a rendering of a double.

Per observation:

```{r}
head(eiod_absolute_threshold(eiod_demo$ghg_kgco2e, grp, "ghg",
                             details = TRUE), 4)
```

## Two cautions specific to this table

**Eutrophication must be supplied in grams.** Eight of the Table 3 cut-offs
were corrected by Intake in October 2026 and differ from the published PDF,
which prints that row in kilograms. If you have a script that divided
eutrophication by 1000 before calling this function, **remove the division**.
See `vignette("eutrophication")`.

**This metric and the relative one answer different questions and will not
agree.** For greenhouse gases the planetary-boundary threshold lies below the
10th percentile of the reference distribution; for water it lies above the
90th. Never use a relative band as a proxy for this result, or the reverse —
`vignette("table4-relative")` shows where each threshold falls.
